**Mainland Southeast Asia** (historically known as **Indochina** and the **Indochinese Peninsula**; abbreviated **MSEA**) is the continental portion of Southeast Asia. It comprises the countries of Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:1-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:4-6) MSEA borders East Asia to the north, South Asia to the west, and Maritime Southeast Asia to the south and east.
The term _Indochina_ (originally _Indo-China_) was coined in the early nineteenth century, emphasizing the historical cultural influence of Indian and Chinese civilizations on the region. The term was later adopted as the name of the colony of French Indochina (present-day Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and parts of China). Today, the term _Mainland Southeast Asia_ is more commonly used, in contrast to Maritime Southeast Asia for the island groups off the coast of the continental region.
1886 map of Indochina, from the Scottish Geographical Magazine

In Indian sources, the earliest name connected with Southeast Asia is _Yāvadvīpa_[ms].[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7) Another possible early name of mainland Southeast Asia was _Suvarṇabhūmi_ ('land of gold'),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-8) a toponym, that appears in many ancient Indian literary sources and Buddhist texts,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-9) but which, along with _Suvarṇadvīpa_ ('island' or 'peninsula of gold'),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7) are also thought to refer to insular Southeast Asia.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7)

The origins of the name Indo-China are usually attributed jointly to the Danish-French geographer Conrad Malte-Brun, who referred to the area as _indo-chinois_ in 1804, and the Scottish linguist John Leyden, who used the term _Indo-Chinese_ to describe the area's inhabitants and their languages in 1808.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-10) The unfamiliar outsiders from Europe thought the region had a dual Indian and Chinese cultural makeup.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) Much of the mainland practiced Theravada Buddhism while the east coast had a Confucian Kingdom (Đại Việt) with a language based on Chinese characters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) However, in reality the mainland was inhabited by about 12 different kingdoms and other territories with an ethnically diverse population descended from 23 different societies dating back to at least the 14th century.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) The French failed to properly recognize this ethnic diversity and simply referred to the region as Indochina.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11)

Scholarly opinions at the time regarding China's and India's historical influence over the area were conflicting, and the term was itself controversial—Malte-Brun himself later argued against its use in a later edition of his _La Nouvelle Géographie universelle_, reasoning that it overemphasized Chinese influence, and suggested _Chin-India_ instead.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-12) Nevertheless, _Indo-China_ had already gained traction and soon supplanted alternative terms such as _Further India_ and the _Peninsula beyond the Ganges_. Later, however, as the French established the colony of French Indochina (covering present-day Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam), use of the term became more restricted to the French colony.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) After the Vietnam War, the term Indochina gradually fell out of use in favor of the more politically correct (Mainland) Southeast Asia.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) Today the area is usually referred to as Mainland Southeast Asia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-14)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:0-2) The regional abbreviation MSEA is used especially in academia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-16)
In biogeography, the Indochinese bioregion is a major region in the Indomalayan realm, and also a phytogeographicalfloristic region in the Oriental Paleotropical Kingdom. It includes the native flora and fauna of all the countries above. The adjacent Malesian Region covers the Maritime Southeast Asian countries, and straddles the Indomalayan and Australasian realms.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-17)

**Mainland Southeast Asia** (historically known as **Indochina** and the **Indochinese Peninsula**; abbreviated **MSEA**) is the continental portion of Southeast Asia. It comprises the countries of Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:1-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:4-6) MSEA borders East Asia to the north, South Asia to the west, and Maritime Southeast Asia to the south and east.
The term _Indochina_ (originally _Indo-China_) was coined in the early nineteenth century, emphasizing the historical cultural influence of Indian and Chinese civilizations on the region. The term was later adopted as the name of the colony of French Indochina (present-day Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and parts of China). Today, the term _Mainland Southeast Asia_ is more commonly used, in contrast to Maritime Southeast Asia for the island groups off the coast of the continental region.
1886 map of Indochina, from the Scottish Geographical Magazine
texts.2: In Indian sources, the earliest name connected with Southeast Asia is _Yāvadvīpa_[ms].[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7) Another possible early name of mainland Southeast Asia was _Suvarṇabhūmi_ ('land of gold'),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-8) a toponym, that appears in many ancient Indian literary sources and Buddhist texts,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-9) but which, along with _Suvarṇadvīpa_ ('island' or 'peninsula of gold'),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7) are also thought to refer to insular Southeast Asia.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7)
texts.3: The origins of the name Indo-China are usually attributed jointly to the Danish-French geographer Conrad Malte-Brun, who referred to the area as _indo-chinois_ in 1804, and the Scottish linguist John Leyden, who used the term _Indo-Chinese_ to describe the area's inhabitants and their languages in 1808.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-10) The unfamiliar outsiders from Europe thought the region had a dual Indian and Chinese cultural makeup.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) Much of the mainland practiced Theravada Buddhism while the east coast had a Confucian Kingdom (Đại Việt) with a language based on Chinese characters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) However, in reality the mainland was inhabited by about 12 different kingdoms and other territories with an ethnically diverse population descended from 23 different societies dating back to at least the 14th century.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) The French failed to properly recognize this ethnic diversity and simply referred to the region as Indochina.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11)
texts.4:
Scholarly opinions at the time regarding China's and India's historical influence over the area were conflicting, and the term was itself controversial—Malte-Brun himself later argued against its use in a later edition of his _La Nouvelle Géographie universelle_, reasoning that it overemphasized Chinese influence, and suggested _Chin-India_ instead.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-12) Nevertheless, _Indo-China_ had already gained traction and soon supplanted alternative terms such as _Further India_ and the _Peninsula beyond the Ganges_. Later, however, as the French established the colony of French Indochina (covering present-day Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam), use of the term became more restricted to the French colony.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) After the Vietnam War, the term Indochina gradually fell out of use in favor of the more politically correct (Mainland) Southeast Asia.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) Today the area is usually referred to as Mainland Southeast Asia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-14)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:0-2) The regional abbreviation MSEA is used especially in academia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-16)
In biogeography, the Indochinese bioregion is a major region in the Indomalayan realm, and also a phytogeographicalfloristic region in the Oriental Paleotropical Kingdom. It includes the native flora and fauna of all the countries above. The adjacent Malesian Region covers the Maritime Southeast Asian countries, and straddles the Indomalayan and Australasian realms.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-17)

**Mainland Southeast Asia** (historically known as **Indochina** and the **Indochinese Peninsula**; abbreviated **MSEA**) is the continental portion of Southeast Asia. It comprises the countries of Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:1-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:4-6) MSEA borders East Asia to the north, South Asia to the west, and Maritime Southeast Asia to the south and east.
The term _Indochina_ (originally _Indo-China_) was coined in the early nineteenth century, emphasizing the historical cultural influence of Indian and Chinese civilizations on the region. The term was later adopted as the name of the colony of French Indochina (present-day Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and parts of China). Today, the term _Mainland Southeast Asia_ is more commonly used, in contrast to Maritime Southeast Asia for the island groups off the coast of the continental region.
1886 map of Indochina, from the Scottish Geographical Magazine

In Indian sources, the earliest name connected with Southeast Asia is _Yāvadvīpa_[ms].[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7) Another possible early name of mainland Southeast Asia was _Suvarṇabhūmi_ ('land of gold'),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-8) a toponym, that appears in many ancient Indian literary sources and Buddhist texts,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-9) but which, along with _Suvarṇadvīpa_ ('island' or 'peninsula of gold'),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7) are also thought to refer to insular Southeast Asia.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-Wheatley-7)

The origins of the name Indo-China are usually attributed jointly to the Danish-French geographer Conrad Malte-Brun, who referred to the area as _indo-chinois_ in 1804, and the Scottish linguist John Leyden, who used the term _Indo-Chinese_ to describe the area's inhabitants and their languages in 1808.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-10) The unfamiliar outsiders from Europe thought the region had a dual Indian and Chinese cultural makeup.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) Much of the mainland practiced Theravada Buddhism while the east coast had a Confucian Kingdom (Đại Việt) with a language based on Chinese characters.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) However, in reality the mainland was inhabited by about 12 different kingdoms and other territories with an ethnically diverse population descended from 23 different societies dating back to at least the 14th century.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) The French failed to properly recognize this ethnic diversity and simply referred to the region as Indochina.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11)

Scholarly opinions at the time regarding China's and India's historical influence over the area were conflicting, and the term was itself controversial—Malte-Brun himself later argued against its use in a later edition of his _La Nouvelle Géographie universelle_, reasoning that it overemphasized Chinese influence, and suggested _Chin-India_ instead.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-12) Nevertheless, _Indo-China_ had already gained traction and soon supplanted alternative terms such as _Further India_ and the _Peninsula beyond the Ganges_. Later, however, as the French established the colony of French Indochina (covering present-day Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam), use of the term became more restricted to the French colony.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) After the Vietnam War, the term Indochina gradually fell out of use in favor of the more politically correct (Mainland) Southeast Asia.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:5-11) Today the area is usually referred to as Mainland Southeast Asia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-14)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-:0-2) The regional abbreviation MSEA is used especially in academia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-16)
In biogeography, the Indochinese bioregion is a major region in the Indomalayan realm, and also a phytogeographicalfloristic region in the Oriental Paleotropical Kingdom. It includes the native flora and fauna of all the countries above. The adjacent Malesian Region covers the Maritime Southeast Asian countries, and straddles the Indomalayan and Australasian realms.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Southeast_Asia#cite_note-17)
